primitives.name: Pseudo-Game Regularization
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model **Pseudo-game regularization.** Add δ fractional wins AND δ fractional losses to *every* unordered pair: augmented log-likelihood l_δ(θ) = Σ_{i<j}{(y_ij+δ)log p_ij + (y_ji+δ)log(1-p_ij)} = l(θ) + δ Σ_{i<j} log{p_ij(1-p_ij)}.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'δ': 'regularization strength (dimensionless)', 'p_ij': 'probability that team i beats team j (dimensionless)', 'θ_i': 'log-odds ability of team i (logit scale)'}
primitives.assumptions: Model assumes logistic link function, paired comparisons, and symmetric pseudo-games between all pairs.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Infinite estimates in disconnected or nearly separated graphs; fails to resolve location nonidentifiability.

layer2.mapping: Induces a penalty kernel equivalent to ridge regression with linear tail behavior, enabling stable estimation in sparse designs.
layer2.telemetry: Shrinkage of extreme log-abilities, convergence of likelihood estimates.

primitives.name: Phantom-Player Regularization
primitives.verbatim_quote: **Phantom-player regularization.** Add an artificial competitor with fixed strength θ_0 = 0; each real competitor receives one pseudo-win + one pseudo-loss vs the phantom, weighted by ρ ≥ 0: l_ρ(θ) = l(θ) + ρ Σ_j [log F(θ_j) + log(1-F(θ_j))].
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'ρ': 'phantom player weight (dimensionless)', 'F': 'cumulative distribution function (logistic or normal)', 'θ_j': 'log-odds ability of team j (logit scale)'}
primitives.assumptions: Fixed phantom strength θ_0 = 0, independent pseudo-observations per team, logistic or normal link function.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Infinite estimates in disconnected graphs; linear penalty avoids over-shrinkage of moderate abilities.

layer2.mapping: Maps to MAP estimation under independent shrinkage priors, offering robustness akin to L1 regularization.
layer2.telemetry: Stabilized extreme ratings, reduced variance in early-season estimates.

primitives.name: Shrinkage Calibration Dial
primitives.verbatim_quote: The phantom-player penalty has *linear* (robust) tails vs ridge's quadratic ones, and both can be fit in plain `glm`; the calibration formula q = (1+δ)/(1+2δ) gives GSE an interpretable shrinkage dial for early-season ratings.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'q': 'fair win probability of a team vs average (dimensionless)', 'δ': 'pseudo-game regularization strength (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Team performance modeled as Bernoulli trials, baseline uniformity assumed.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Nonlinear mapping invalidates direct inference for large δ; requires calibration for interpretability.

layer2.mapping: Provides a scalar dial to tune regularization strength based on desired shrinkage level, linking empirical win probabilities to model parameters.
layer2.telemetry: Interpretable shrinkage factor, calibrated via win probability queries.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of the paper lies in reformulating regularization in Bradley–Terry models as pseudo-observations. Pseudo-games add δ fractional wins/losses to all pairs, yielding a log-likelihood penalty proportional to log(p_ij(1−p_ij)), which shrinks differences in abilities toward equality. This is mathematically equivalent to a prior on pairwise differences, leading to a kernel with linear tails. Phantom-player regularization introduces a fixed-strength phantom team, adding pseudo-outcomes to each real team, resulting in a penalty term involving log(F(θ_j)(1−F(θ_j))). This induces a MAP estimate under independent shrinkage priors, offering robustness similar to L1 regularization. Both methods avoid infinite estimates in disconnected graphs, unlike standard maximum likelihood. The phantom-player approach is shown to approximate ridge regression locally, but with superior robustness due to its linear penalty structure. The calibration formula q = (1+δ)/(1+2δ) allows users to map desired win probabilities back to δ, providing an intuitive interface for tuning regularization strength in early-season ratings.
